She lives in Snyder, Texas. Having originally been settled by the Flathead people, it was later annexed by a goods and services company that needed a municipality. In 1922, the state allowed civilians to retain townsites that were unincorporated. The state had released a new survey grid of lots that would become streets and businesses. The company's executive council opposed becoming a municipality, and so threw the carefully considered plan into a bonfire. One of the town streets now meanders for no particular reason, and a lot that was supposed to be a filling station is the rear parking space for a dental business.

There was a gunfight in the vacant lot behind what was meant to be the post office, and it became the skating rink.

Snyder's population peaked at twelve thousand during World War II. Homes were thrown up quick, on lots that were crammed together too closely. The goal was cheap housing. The overall look of downtown is that of a Matchbox 1940s--1949 Austin twist 'n go set, painted mostly brown and gray. The new bits that have been added over the years resemble models the company zoned original before realizing it had overskirted itself, but the scaffolding is different.

Texas sensibly does not consider Snyder rich. But it is not poor. Average household income is $42,406. Medicare/Medicaid recipients come from Rooke and Lee. In 2018, 2.7 percent of the residents were arrested for DUI/DWI. Thirty percent are roofless. But then, they don't all have dogs.

The city likes itself, as such places do. It has the sort of corruption commonly found in towns that produce a steady amount of Vitamin C. On an October evening in the 1940s, someone drove a car through the doors of the Inverness Hotel, then set it on fire. The Inverness was a beautiful cream-colored beach hotel at West 1370, between Eldridge Avenue and Lake Michigan. It was packed with Jazz Age vacationers: senior clerks with their wives, viceroys from Britain, jazz outfits from New Orleans on their way to the Roadhouse at 49th and Broadway. The car was going too fast, turned wild, cruised past the laundry and the pool deck and seaside stables, still speeding hard with flames coming out of it like bombs. It crashed into some dunes behind the third hole of the local golf course, then crashed into a storage barn that exploded in a huge fireball.

The golf course (and, therefore, the dunes) were gone now, replaced by 46th Family Shopping Center, which opened in 1964 in the first round of insurgent suburban development that would reach all the way to Racine by the beginning of this century. The department stores and discount shops of 46th were superseded and covered first by the Wal-Mart Supercenter and then by the enclosed-city big-box mall built by Target. The Beacon Hotel's grounds, which had once backed up against 46th and 38th streets, were paved over and became the parking lot for the outpatient cancer clinic, Steele Memorial Hospital and 3M World Headquarters Expressway. The Beaumont-Carreras Hotel, which once occupied rock bluffs along the lake opposite the Inverness, was replaced by the Glacier Bay Fitness Club, the polling station at McKinley Avenue Elementary and the parking lot for the new county courthouse.

Fifteen people arrived at the King County Election Center in Renton at eight o'clock on behalf of 39,784 families. They share one thing with all the other Americans who have just arrived here today: They are committed. They work hard, they watch their budgets, and they idle the equivalent of 35 year-round full-time vehicle hours for an average 15 minutes of downtime while we make sure everything is right for their vote.

We invite them in, one at a time.

If the Voter Services Assistant handling the door loves animals, she can tell dogs and cats apart in an instant, not just by species, but by gender, breed, and temperament. Maybe it's because of their own pets. Or they've grown up on farms. Or they've dealt with a traumatized stray.

Before they get their badges, our final-hiring layers are anonymous: The candidates are called "Candidate Grizzly"; "First Preliminary Alligator 5" and "Final Tenth Fox 7," who goes to work as Natasha Batipaka.

As they leave their training, they all get new names. Natasha likes "Super Tortoise" or "Black Panther."

Black and brown people, the poorer ones, are the pilots of close elections: it's not always the liberals who change, after all, who know just how many votes they will turn away when they're on the edge of being kicked out of their apartments. Everyone blasts the post election: extra work for election workers and disabled voters like Grandma. But it's better than voting no and sleeping through the rest, her daughter pointed out. A protest is one thing.

Keisha stayed home. She didn't talk to her mother or Jalen. It got hard to answer when they asked how she'd voted. Grandma texted to see how she dealt with the losses. She didn't say. She heard nothing from her neighbors who'd actually voted, barely, double tapping the ballot till they made it to Keisha just to satisfy the app. Some day, she saw, they would just tap away harder.

Keisha had let him go to the polling place by himself, to hand in his very serious paper ballot, and she hadn't gone to vote at all.

She could not even look at them without feeling jealous of all the mothers who could take their kids to things like this, who had the time, the gas, the already-crumpled twenty she'd spent for gas even though her credit card payment was late, and whose kids came home with notes about science fairs and track meets and extra time on the reading goals.

She let herself imagine it, just for a moment: the taste of her words, the sound of her voice. "You just let that little boy watch a building fall down slowly, just fall down slowly and crush everything in it." The joy of never declaring her candidacy, never signing a single petition, never being invited to a single meeting or asked to raise a single buck.

She turned the wheel for the car wash. Drive-thru. She could not bring herself to touch those grimy buttons that never worked right, so she drove through and swiped her credit card.

At home she shed her clothes and turned up the heat to ninety degrees and let the water run in the shower until it felt like somebody had cranked one of those old rotary dials all the way up. She got in and sat and held the bottle of shampoo you rubbed into your scalp until somebody came to get you out. When she finished, she stood, the white towel slung over her shoulder. The house was as silent as it had been two hours ago, until she walked through the kitchen into the living room and heard the creak of the front porch then Jalen's voice, clear and bright and liquid as water, saying, "Lydia, you can come in now.”

Roosevelt Elementary is two miles from their neighborhood. It's called Roosevelt because it was built the year Kennedy was assassinated. It’s a poor neighborhood and, ever since Columbine, the school careened between lockdowns and lockdown drills. The kids spent most of their time just trying to calm each other down from the school’s extreme anxiety. Last year they finally doubled the counseling staff to two part-time employees, 70 percent of whom needed to be on message all the time or else they were at risk of triggering a PTSD episode in one of the kids. The modern American elementary school is the place where children learn to numb like their parents learned to numb.

Roosevelt had its share of problems — the principal would say it was 70 percent teachers, 20 percent overcrowding, and 10 percent kids. This year the roof was a problem, and every winter the heat was a problem too. But there were good parts — especially the fifth-grade teacher, and music class, and gym class if you could get away with hiding in the hallway while the other kids played whatever game middle-school kids played nowadays.

Last spring the gym teacher, who was also charged with running the energy program for the school district, had a rare moment of insight. One day they were outside for PE, and she saw some kids exploring an air vent behind the gym. She considered ordering them back inside but thought they looked cold and tired, so she cast a blind eye.

Two days later the gym roof collapsed, but it happened on a Saturday, when the only occupancy the gym got was from the 47-person church on the trust fall...whatever that was....folks. A miracle.

Later, when everyone counted their blessings, they decided that they would vote on a $28 million bond to replace the gym and fix the heat. Because the gym was also the auditorium where they had graduation and stuff, so that seemed good, too. The bond had been a tough sell. But they’d run the numbers, and voters were stupid but they were also practical. The average mill levy would be $1.22, which meant that, on average, people would vote yes if they had been in the neighborhood for six years or more. These were the voters who were likeliest to care: they all wanted new roads, and the rest either voted once every four or six years or they didn’t vote at all.

She opened her door and hurried across the wet parking lot, trying not to splash water up her pant legs. The man at the entrance checked her ID, and a woman directed her to the second table from the front. Keisha signed the check-in sheet, and the poll worker handed her a ballot and a blue pen.

Keisha looked down.

It was a paper ballot, not the electronic kind she was used to. The instructions were printed at the top: "FOLD HERE BEFORE YOU BEGIN. FOLDING ALLOWS YOU TO SEE BOTH SIDES OF THE BALLOT AS YOU VOTE."

She glanced at the clock mounted in the corner of the wall: 7:55. Her right shoulder was already aching. Her back would be worse tomorrow. The house was quiet. Nobody needed her right now but herself.

Nelson Davila with his kid in the stroller, saying that even if the bond failed they'd find a way to improve the school. \]
Given that the expenses were $300:
